Sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose, and the link is unusual.
In most disaccharides one anomeric carbon joins to an ordinary hydroxyl, leaving the other
anomeric carbon free. In sucrose *both* anomeric carbons are used.
The anomeric carbon of glucose is C-1; the anomeric carbon of fructose, a ketose, is C-2.
The linkage is therefore C-1 of α-glucose to C-2 of β-fructose, written α-1,2-glycosidic.
Because neither anomeric carbon is left free, no open-chain aldehyde form can appear.
That is why sucrose is a *non-reducing* sugar — it gives no reaction with Tollens' or Fehling's —
while maltose and lactose, which keep one free anomeric carbon, are reducing.
∴ C-1 of α-glucose and C-2 of β-fructose.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|55||0|0.s:
Match each hormone to its gland and composition.
Insulin — a peptide hormone from the pancreas, built of amino acids; no iodine.
Testosterone — a steroid hormone from the testes; carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only.
Adrenaline — a catecholamine from the adrenal medulla; again no iodine.
Thyroxine — secreted by the thyroid gland, and it is an iodinated derivative of the amino acid
tyrosine. Its formula is C₁₅H₁₁I₄NO₄, carrying four iodine atoms, which is why it is also called T4.
This is exactly why dietary iodine matters: without it the thyroid cannot make thyroxine, the
gland enlarges trying to compensate, and the result is goitre. Hence iodised salt.
∴ thyroxine.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|56||0|0:
Find the false statement.
(A) True — thiamine (B₁) is found in yeast, milk, green vegetables and cereals; its deficiency
causes beri-beri.
(B) True — pyridoxine (B₆) deficiency causes convulsions and anaemia.
(C) True — scurvy is the deficiency disease of vitamin C, which citrus fruits and green leafy
vegetables supply.
(D) False — xerophthalmia, the drying of the cornea, is caused by a deficiency of **vitamin A**,
not vitamin D. Vitamin A deficiency also gives night blindness.
Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults, because without it
calcium is not absorbed properly and the bones soften.
∴ statement (D) is wrong.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|57||0|0.s:
Novolac is a phenol–formaldehyde resin, made by condensing phenol with formaldehyde under
*acidic* conditions.
The reaction is an electrophilic substitution on the ring: formaldehyde attacks at the ortho and
para positions to give hydroxymethyl phenol, which then condenses with another phenol molecule,
losing water and forming a –CH₂– bridge between two rings.
Repeating this gives a linear chain, and that linear, soluble polymer is Novolac — used in paints.
Heating Novolac with more formaldehyde cross-links the chains into Bakelite, which is a
three-dimensional thermosetting solid.
(B) melamine with formaldehyde gives melamine–formaldehyde resin, (C) butadiene with styrene
gives Buna-S and (D) butadiene with acrylonitrile gives Buna-N.
∴ phenol and formaldehyde.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|58||0|0:
A polymer is biodegradable if microorganisms can break its backbone, which generally means
the chain contains ester or amide linkages that can be hydrolysed.
(A) and (B) are the same material, PHBV — a copolymer of 3-hydroxybutanoic acid and
3-hydroxypentanoic acid joined by ester links. It is biodegradable and used for packaging and
controlled drug release.
(C) Nylon 2–nylon 6 is an alternating polyamide of glycine and aminocaproic acid; its amide links
are hydrolysable, so it too is biodegradable.
(D) Glyptal is made from ethylene glycol and phthalic acid. It is a heavily cross-linked polyester
resin, and that dense cross-linking leaves nothing for an enzyme to attack.
∴ glyptal is not biodegradable.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|59||0|0.s:
Antibiotics are divided by what they do to the bacterium.
Bactericidal — they kill the organism outright.
Bacteriostatic — they only stop it multiplying, leaving the body's immune system to clear it.
Erythromycin, tetracycline and chloramphenicol all act by binding the bacterial ribosome and
blocking protein synthesis. That halts growth without killing, so all three are bacteriostatic.
Ofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone. It inhibits DNA gyrase, so the bacterial DNA cannot be unwound
and replicated, and the cell dies. That makes it bactericidal.
Penicillin and aminoglycosides are the other familiar bactericidal examples.
∴ ofloxacin.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|1||0|0.s:
For a first order reaction the half-life is constant, so just count how many have passed.
Number of half-lives n = total time / t½ = 240 / 60 = 4
After each half-life the amount left is halved:
60 min ⇒ 50%
120 min ⇒ 25%
180 min ⇒ 12.5%
240 min ⇒ 6.25%
Or in one step: fraction left = (½)ⁿ = (½)⁴ = 1/16 = 0.0625 = 6.25%
∴ 6.25% remains.

A colligative property depends only on the *number* of solute particles in solution, not on what
they are. There are four of them:
relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point and
osmotic pressure.
So (1), (3) and (4) are all colligative.
Optical activity is the rotation of plane-polarised light, and it depends entirely on the *nature*
of the molecule — specifically on whether it is chiral. A solution of a chiral substance rotates
light whatever its concentration; an achiral one never does, however much you dissolve.
It is a property of the particle, not a count of particles.
∴ optical activity is not a colligative property.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|6||0|0.s:
A primary cell runs its reaction once and is then finished — a dry cell, for example.
A secondary cell is one in which the electrode reaction can be reversed, so it can be recharged.
The crucial detail is the direction of the charging current.
While discharging, the cell drives electrons out of its negative electrode through the circuit.
To recharge it you must push electrons back the way they came, so the external current has to
be passed *in the opposite direction* to the discharge current. That reverses the electrode
reactions and regenerates the original reactants.
In a lead storage battery, discharge turns both electrodes to PbSO₄; charging in the opposite
direction converts them back to Pb and PbO₂.
Option (2), recharging in the same direction, would simply continue discharging it.
∴ it can be recharged by passing current through it in the opposite direction.
